title: Righteous Authority
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 5 of 40
content:
I spent the next morning taking apart Paladin Danse’s rifle.

Technically it was my rifle now.

Emotionally, it still felt like handling someone else’s coat.

Righteous Authority lay in pieces across the workbench at Cambridge Police Station: focusing lens, capacitor, barrel assembly, stock, screws lined in a row because I was not an animal. The modifications were careful and practical. Nothing decorative. Nothing added unless it improved function.

It looked exactly like something Danse would build.

He appeared beside me halfway through reassembly.

I did not hear him approach because, for once, he was out of power armor.

That was disorienting enough that I nearly dropped a spring.

Without the steel shell he was still broad, still carried himself with military rigidity, but he looked more human in the simple Brotherhood uniform. Tired, too. There were shadows beneath his eyes I had not been able to see behind the helmet.

“You’re changing the focusing array,” he said.

“Good morning to you too.”

“That array is calibrated.”

“For your grip.”

“It’s adjustable.”

“So am I.”

He leaned over the bench.

His shoulder came close enough to mine that I smelled soap, gun oil, and the metallic scent that clung to people who spent too much time inside powered armor.

I forgot what I was doing for one entire second.

Danse noticed the part in my hand.

“You installed that backward.”

I looked down.

I had.

“Testing you.”

“Of course.”

He reached past me and corrected it.

His forearm brushed mine.

The contact was ordinary.

My reaction to it was stupid.

I stepped sideways under the pretense of reaching for a tool.

Danse continued as if nothing had happened.

“Your modification is sound, but shorten the stock by half an inch. You’re compensating for the length every time you shoulder it.”

“You watched me that closely?”

“I watch everyone under my command.”

“I’m not under your command.”

His mouth tightened.

“Not officially.”

That stopped me.

He looked irritated with himself.

Then he straightened.

“I want to offer you a position.”

I turned fully toward him.

“What kind?”

“The Brotherhood is always looking for capable people. You’ve already demonstrated that you can handle yourself in combat and that you understand technology.”

“Understand is generous.”

“You took apart a custom laser rifle after one night of owning it.”

“Curiosity.”

“Technical curiosity is useful.”

“So you’re recruiting me.”

“Yes.”

“Is this the speech where you tell me I’ll be saving humanity?”

“If you’d like.”

I laughed.

He did not.

Then, unexpectedly, he sat on the edge of the opposite workbench.

“I’m not going to pretend the Brotherhood is perfect.”

That was not the sentence I expected.

Danse looked toward the front of the station where Haylen was working the transmitter.

“But it gave me something I didn’t have before. Structure. Training. People I could depend on. A reason to believe surviving could mean more than getting through another day.”

The humor left me.

“That’s what purpose means to you.”

“Yes.”

Not slogans.

Not doctrine.

A place where an orphaned scavenger had been told he belonged.

I looked back down at the weapon.

“Rhys hates me.”

“Rhys distrusts anyone who isn’t Brotherhood.”

“That is a generous interpretation of his personality.”

Danse’s mouth twitched.

“He’s a good soldier.”

“I didn’t say he wasn’t.”

“Haylen likes you.”

“Haylen has taste.”

This time the smile happened.

Brief, but undeniable.

“I’m undecided,” he said.

“Cruel.”

“I said what I said.”

I finished the rifle and lifted it to my shoulder.

The shorter stock fit better.

Danse nodded.

“Better.”

“You were right.”

“I’m aware.”

“Do you practice being unbearable?”

“No practice necessary.”

I stared at him.

He realized what he had said a heartbeat later.

Haylen, who had absolutely been listening from the next room, choked on a laugh.

Danse looked offended by his own joke.

I liked him instantly more for it.

The transmitter crackled that afternoon.

Not a clean message. Barely words. But a response.

Haylen sat upright so quickly her chair rolled backward.

“Paladin!”

Danse crossed the room in three strides.

Static filled the station.

Then a voice emerged, distant and broken.

Brotherhood call signs. Coordinates. Confirmation.

Home, as far as Danse was concerned, speaking through the noise.

I watched his face change.

Relief first.

Then discipline locked back into place.

He began issuing instructions immediately. Record the transmission. Confirm power levels. Prepare a full report. Inventory supplies. Check ammunition.

He was happiest when there was something to do with a feeling.

That was useful information.

Later, when the station settled and Rhys had finally stopped complaining about his leg, I found Danse alone in the garage inspecting the damaged plates of his power armor.

“You going to sleep?” I asked.

“Eventually.”

“That means no.”

“I have maintenance to finish.”

“You almost got cooked alive yesterday.”

“I’m aware.”

“You fought ghouls before that.”

“I remember.”

“You also walked several miles in a metal suit that weighs more than a brahmin.”

“Your point?”

“My point is that exhaustion is not a moral virtue.”

Danse stopped tightening a bolt.

For a second I thought I had crossed the line again.

Then he set the wrench down.

“You always this persistent?”

“Yes.”

“I was afraid of that.”

I leaned against the workbench.

“Go sleep. I can finish checking the seals.”

“No.”

“Danse.”

He looked at me sharply.

It was the first time I had used his name without the title.

The garage went strangely quiet.

I had not meant anything by it.

Or I had meant too many things by it and none of them were safe to inspect.

His eyes stayed on mine.

Then he looked down at the wrench.

“Fine,” he said.

I blinked.

“That worked?”

“Don’t get used to it.”

He stood.

At the doorway he paused.

“The left shoulder actuator sticks under heavy load.”

“I noticed.”

“The replacement coupling is in the red toolbox.”

“Go to bed.”

His expression softened almost invisibly.

“Yes, ma’am,” he started, then stopped before committing to a gendered honorific, scowled at the linguistic problem, and settled on, “Civilian.”

I grinned.

“Good night, Paladin.”

He left shaking his head.

I turned back to the power armor.

There are intimate things in the Commonwealth that have nothing to do with skin.

Knowing which joint in a man’s armor catches when he is tired, I would learn, was one of them.

Later that afternoon, he caught me cleaning carbon scoring from the forearm plate.

“You missed lunch,” he said.

“So did you.”

“I was conducting an inventory.”

“I was conducting maintenance.”

“That is not the same thing.”

“It is if we both forgot to eat.”

Danse looked toward the station’s improvised kitchen, then back at the armor.

“I did not forget.”

“You strategically postponed chewing?”

“Yes.”

I laughed.

He disappeared into the back room and returned with two dented tins and a packet of crackers old enough to qualify as archaeological evidence.

He placed one ration beside me.

“What’s this?”

“Food.”

“I recognize the broad category.”

“You criticized my meal schedule.”

“So you brought me yours?”

“I brought you a separate ration.”

“Which you definitely planned to eat before I pointed out you hadn’t.”

Danse sat on the edge of the desk and opened his tin with unnecessary concentration.

“I’m reconsidering the wisdom of rewarding your observations.”

We ate in companionable silence for almost a minute.

Then I asked, “Why that rifle?”

His eyes dropped to Righteous Authority where it rested across the bench.

“It’s reliable.”

“That’s not why you looked like you were handing me a medal when you gave it to me.”

Danse stopped chewing.

“I did not look like that.”

“You did a little.”

He set the ration down.

“I gave it to you because you earned it.”

The words came stiffly, as if he disliked having to explain praise once it had already escaped.

“You entered a Brotherhood operation with no obligation to us. You followed orders under fire, adapted when plans changed, and did not abandon me when the engine room became… complicated.”

“Complicated is one word for it.”

“I had expected you to retreat.”

“Were you disappointed when I didn’t?”

“No.”

His gaze stayed on mine.

“Quite the opposite.”

Heat climbed somewhere beneath my collar. I focused on the rifle because the rifle was safe.

“So it’s not a recruitment bribe?”

His mouth twitched.

“No.”

“Not even a little?”

“The Brotherhood could use someone with your abilities.”

“There it is.”

“That does not make the weapon a bribe.”

“Recruitment gift.”

“Recognition of service.”

“Very romantic phrasing.”

Danse nearly inhaled a cracker.

The coughing fit lasted long enough for Haylen to look over from the transmitter.

“Everything all right, Paladin?”

“Yes.”

His answer came much too quickly.

I stared very seriously at the rifle.

Haylen’s eyes moved from Danse to me and back again.

Her smile was terrible.

“I’m sure.”

She returned to her work.

Danse lowered his voice.

“You did that intentionally.”

“I have no idea what you mean.”

“Outstanding.”

I bit down on my grin.

He finished his ration, but his ears stayed red for the rest of the meal.

That was the day I learned the Brotherhood’s power armor had less defensive value against flirting than advertised.

prose_fingerprint: emotionally direct without flattening emotion into exposition
ground abstract feelings in concrete physical details, objects, weather, rooms, gestures, and sensory anchors
alternate compact emotional beats with fuller reflective paragraphs
let dialogue carry relationship pressure while narration carries interior consequence
use humor and ordinary practical actions to make vulnerable scenes feel lived-in rather than staged
favor character-specific reactions and small remembered details over generic declarations
allow grief, identity, survival, belonging, home, change, vulnerability, care, and autonomy to recur as thematic pressure
end scenes or chapters on an emotional consequence, changed understanding, concrete image, callback, or forward pull
preserve first-person immediacy and avoid omniscient knowledge outside Jasper's perception
use semicolons selectively for linked thoughts rather than mechanically
dialogue_fingerprint: continuous dialogue should sound conversational rather than like alternating speeches
interrupt dialogue with gestures, environment, hesitation, humor, and internal reaction
let characters dodge, misunderstand, tease, repair, and return to earlier wording
do not make every character equally eloquent, equally dominant, or equally emotionally transparent
relationship_fingerprint: slow burn must accumulate evidence: remembered preferences, repaired conflict, shared routines, private jokes, and practical care
attraction should not erase plot, outside obligations, individual goals, or conflict
vulnerability is strongest when it changes later behavior
after an intense/private interlude, resume with reconnection, humor, care, consequences, memory updates, and the next plot beat rather than treating intimacy as a reset
